sources.notes: Crowd-scraped Wiktionary gold, 681 rows. Consulted only to settle which reading a letter takes where the orthographies overlap, to order the ambiguous candidate lists, and to establish that tone is not written: ⟨p⟩ is [k͡p] in 29 of 29 words (⟨pataki⟩ and ⟨kpataki⟩ are the same word), ⟨hw⟩ is [ɣʷ] in 9 of 9, ⟨h⟩ splits [h] 31 / [x] 18 / [ɣ] 7, ⟨d⟩ splits [d] 37 / [ɖ] 16, ⟨ṣ⟩ is [ʃ] with [t͡ʃ] in the ⟨Ajaṣẹ⟩/⟨Ajacɛ⟩ type, ⟨r⟩ is [ɾ] and [l] in equal numbers over 6 rows, a vowel written after ⟨m n ny⟩ is nasal in 130 of 155 cases, and tone is written in 3 of 681 entries.

notes: Gun / Gungbe (Gbe, Benin and south-western Nigeria). Two Latin orthographies are in use for the same language and this spec describes both. The Benin national alphabet (Africa-alphabet based, closely following Fon) writes ⟨ɛ⟩ /ɛ/, ⟨ɔ⟩ /ɔ/, ⟨ɖ⟩ /ɖ/, ⟨x⟩ /x/, ⟨xw⟩ /xʷ/, ⟨hw⟩ /ɣʷ/, ⟨gb⟩ /ɡ͡b/, ⟨kp⟩ /k͡p/, ⟨c⟩ /t͡ʃ/, ⟨ny⟩ /ɲ/. The Nigerian orthography is Yoruba-based and writes those same sounds ⟨ẹ ọ d h wh ṣ p⟩; ⟨p⟩ there is the labial-velar /k͡p/, not a plain stop, which Gbe has only in loans, and ⟨ṣ⟩ carries its Yoruba value /ʃ/ but also stands in for ⟨c⟩ /t͡ʃ/ (⟨Ajaṣẹ⟩ = ⟨Ajacɛ⟩). Because the two conventions overlap, ⟨d⟩ stands for /d/ or /ɖ/ and ⟨h⟩ for /x/, /ɣ/ or /h/, and the spec offers both readings to the lattice instead of guessing; /x/ and /ɣ/ themselves vary dialectally as [x~χ~h] and [ɣ~ʁ]. ⟨r⟩ is /ɾ/ or /l/: /l/ is realised as a trill after laminal alveolars, palato-alveolars and palatals, which is the only environment ⟨r⟩ is written in. A vowel followed by a CODA ⟨n⟩ is nasal and the ⟨n⟩ is not a segment (⟨xlan⟩ [xlã]); an ⟨n⟩ that opens the next syllable is an ordinary consonant (⟨ayɔnu⟩ [ajɔnũ]), and ⟨nn⟩ is the two together, not a geminate (⟨sunnu⟩ [sũnũ]). Only /i u ɛ ɔ a/ nasalise — /e o/ have no nasal counterparts, so a coda nasal after them survives as a consonant (⟨ogongo⟩ [oɡonɡo]; the place assimilation that gives [oɡoŋɡo] is not modelled). Every written nasal consonant entails a nasal nucleus after it, because none of them is an independent phoneme before a nasal vowel: [m] and [n] are what /b/ and /ɖ/ become there, and [ɲ] is /j/ there, in free variation with [j̃] (⟨mi⟩ [mĩ], ⟨nyɔ⟩ [ɲɔ̃]). Gungbe is tonal (H/M/L), but tone is not written in either orthography and is therefore not recoverable from ordinary spelling.
